content: 1. In one observational (non-randomized) study involving 820 participants, the incidence of the outcome was 723 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 614 per 1,000, with 108 fewer cases per 1,000 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 159 fewer to 51 fewer). The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to a serious risk of bias. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of mass drug administration (MDA) on the outcome. 2. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving 144,422 participants, the incidence was 57 per 1,000 in the control group and 35 per 1,000 in the intervention group. The certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate due to serious imprecision. MDA probably reduces the incidence of the outcome. 3. In another RCT involving 1,497 participants, the incidence was 2 per 1,000 in the control group and 1 per 1,000 in the intervention group. The certainty of the evidence was rated as low due to very serious imprecision. MDA may result in little to no difference in the incidence of the outcome. 4. In a randomized controlled trial involving 3,154 participants, the incidence was 483 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 570 per 1,000, with 87 more cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 53 fewer to 271 more). The certainty of the evidence was rated as low due to very serious imprecision. MDA may result in little to no difference in the outcome. 5. In an observational (non-randomized) study involving 517 participants, the incidence was 418 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 251 per 1,000, with 167 fewer cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 188 fewer to 138 fewer). The certainty of the evidence was rated as low. MDA may reduce the prevalence of the outcome. 6. In another observational study involving 3,261 participants, the incidence was 431 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 332 per 1,000, with 99 fewer cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 129 fewer to 69 fewer). The certainty of the evidence was rated as low. MDA may reduce the prevalence of the outcome. 7. In a randomized controlled trial involving 90 participants, the incidence was 133 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 333 per 1,000, with 200 more cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 39 fewer to 572 more). The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to very serious inconsistency. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of MDA on adverse events among individuals who received MDA. 8. In a randomized controlled trial involving 336,821 participants, the incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs) was 2 per 1,000 in the control group. The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of MDA on SAEs among individuals who received MDA. 9. In a systematic review of five cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) and seven non-randomized studies (NRSs) conducted in eight countries, MDA was assessed for its impact on the transmission of Plasmodium vivax. The cRCTs used dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP), with four studies also administering single low-dose primaquine. However, none of the cRCTs used sufficient dosages of an 8-aminoquinoline to achieve radical cure of P. vivax hypnozoites. One study provided a single round of MDA, while the other four conducted three rounds. Among the NRSs, only one study reported radical cure of P. vivax. The designs of MDA interventions in the NRSs varied significantly, ranging from a single round to 24 weekly rounds. 10. Meta-analysis of data from the cRCTs suggested that MDA may reduce P. vivax prevalence 1–3 months after the last round of MDA. However, no impact was observed on the prevalence of P. vivax at later time points. The certainty of evidence from the NRSs was very low across all time periods and outcomes. Data from a cRCT that did not provide an 8-aminoquinoline medicine indicated that MDA probably did not increase the rate of severe adverse events within 0–3 months. 11. In an observational study involving 1,024 participants, the incidence was 231 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 42 per 1,000, with 189 fewer cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 208 fewer to 155 fewer). The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of MDA on the outcome. 12. In a randomized controlled trial involving 6,911 participants, the incidence of serious adverse events was 3 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 5 per 1,000, with 2 more cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 1 fewer to 8 more). The certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate due to serious imprecision. MDA probably results in little to no difference in serious adverse events between 4–12 months. 13. Two NRSs provided data on mass relapse prevention (MRP) for P. vivax. These studies were conducted in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea in 2002 and the Republic of Azerbaijan in 1970–1971. Both studies reported decreases in the incidence of P. vivax 1–3 months after the intervention. However, the risk of bias in these studies was considered very serious. Both studies also found a decrease in the incidence of P. vivax 4–12 months after the intervention, with one study reporting a decrease in prevalence during this period. The overall certainty of the evidence was graded as very low due to potential biases resulting from the study designs. 14. In an observational study involving 218,308 participants, the incidence was 111 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 9 per 1,000, with 10 fewer cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 11 fewer to 10 fewer). The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to very serious risk of bias. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of MRP on the incidence of P. vivax infection between 4–12 months. 15. In another observational study involving 6,710 participants, the incidence was 4 per 1,000 in the control group and 0 per 1,000 in the intervention group. The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to risk of bias. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of MRP on the prevalence of P. vivax infection between 4–12 months. 16. In an observational study involving 416,617 participants, the incidence was 13 per 1,000 in the control group. The difference observed was 3 per 1,000, with 10 fewer cases per 1,000 (95% CI: 11 fewer to 10 fewer). The certainty of the evidence was rated as very low due to very serious risk of bias. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of MRP on the incidence of P. vivax infection between 4–12 months. 17. Adverse event data from one study involving 333,946 participants indicated no cases of severe hemolysis. Side effects were reported in less than 4% of the population. However, the overall certainty of the evidence was graded as very low due to potential biases in the study designs. These interpretations reflect the detailed findings and limitations of the studies, emphasizing the uncertainty and variability in the evidence regarding the effects of MDA and MRP on P. vivax transmission and related outcomes.
